strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: estimating Fisher information without constructing the full parameter-output Jacobian. The detached, probability-weighted random loss provides a simple implementation using one backward pass per probe.

The estimator's unbiasedness and the diagonal variance formulas in Proposition 12 are convincing. The bound Std(F_ii estimate) <= sqrt(2) F_ii is a useful conditional guarantee, and the analysis explicitly distinguishes Gaussian and Rademacher probes.

The decomposition through the categorical Fisher matrix provides a coherent framework for deriving spectral bounds and transferring them to parameter space. Detailed proofs and illustrative experiments on pretrained and fine-tuned DistilBERT are provided.
weaknesses: The novelty is insufficiently established. Much of the deterministic analysis follows directly from standard interlacing, trace inequalities, and congruence transformations; the estimator is a random projection of a Fisher factor followed by an outer product. The paper needs a precise comparison with existing stochastic curvature-factor propagation and sampled Gauss–Newton/Fisher methods, including the cited Botev et al. and BackPACK work. The assertion that the bounds improve on prior work is not supported by explicit comparisons under matching assumptions.

Section 4.1 compares different sources of randomness. Its heavy-tailed Monte Carlo example includes sampling inputs from a population, whereas Proposition 12 conditions on a fixed dataset and randomizes only the probes. Input subsampling would introduce additional variance for the proposed estimator too. At theta = 0 in the example, sampling labels on fixed inputs actually gives exact per-input Fisher contributions. Thus this example does not establish the claimed advantage over Monte Carlo at a matched target and computational budget.

The evaluation does not measure estimation accuracy. Figures 1 and 2 show marginal density plots from 128 examples and 10 probes, without exact Fisher references, quantitative errors, repeated-run uncertainty, or matched-cost Monte Carlo comparisons. With only two or four classes, exact diagonal references on a manageable subset would be feasible. There are also no timing, memory, probe-count, or downstream experiments supporting the practical scalability and utility claims.

The quality guarantee is substantially narrower than the full-tensor claims suggest. Proposition 12 controls individual diagonal entries, not relative errors of arbitrary off-diagonal entries or matrix approximation quality. For Gaussian probes, Var(F_ij estimate) = F_ii F_jj + F_ij^2, so off-diagonal relative variance can diverge when F_ij approaches zero. A single estimate is rank one; unbiasedness alone does not make it an accurate full or block Fisher approximation.

There are incorrect mathematical statements requiring correction. Lemma 3 prints 1 - ||p|| - p_(C-1), whereas its proof requires 1 - ||p||^2 - p_(C-1); the printed bound is false even for p = (1/2, 1/2). The discussion after Lemma 2 also confuses maximal/minimal elements with greatest/least elements in the Löwner order. The dominant rank-one component does not dominate all other rank-one lower bounds.

The practical low-rank construction does not preserve its advertised deterministic guarantee automatically. Section 4.3 permits a fixed number of power iterations, but a Rayleigh quotient times an approximate eigenvector outer product need not be a Löwner lower bound of the core matrix. No residual-based correction or approximation analysis connects this implementation to Proposition 6.

Several interpretations of the deterministic bounds are overstated. Vanishing trimmed probabilities imply vanishing parameter-space error only with suitable control of the Jacobian, and smaller upper bounds do not establish uniformly smaller realized approximation error. The experiments do not investigate these qualifications or demonstrate when the bounds are informative.

strengths: The estimator in Equations (2)–(3) is simple and unbiased, using a scalar surrogate and one backward pass without explicitly constructing the parameter-output Jacobian.
Proposition 12 provides a useful diagonal variance guarantee: the coefficient of variation is at most sqrt(2), with an explicit improvement for Rademacher probes over Gaussian probes.
The core-space formulation organizes several useful spectral and approximation bounds, with detailed derivations in the appendices.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish estimation accuracy or practical advantage. Figures 1–2 show distributions of estimated diagonal entries, without exact-reference errors, repeated-run uncertainty, accuracy versus probe count, or runtime and memory comparisons. Both experiments use DistilBERT, and SST-2 has a rank-one core where the proposed low-rank approximation is already exact. No downstream benefit is demonstrated.

The Monte Carlo comparison in Section 4.1 mixes different sources of randomness. Its heavy-tailed counterexample concerns sampling inputs from a population, whereas Proposition 12 conditions on a fixed dataset and averages only over probes. Input subsampling would also introduce additional variance for the proposed estimator. This comparison therefore does not establish the claimed general advantage under matched data access and computational budgets.

Novelty is insufficiently established. The estimator follows directly from the standard identity E[(Aξ)(Aξ)^T] = AA^T, and much of the deterministic analysis applies classical interlacing and trace inequalities. The paper needs a precise comparison with existing stochastic curvature propagation and sampled Fisher/Gauss–Newton methods, including the cited BackPACK and practical Gauss–Newton work.

Some mathematical claims are incorrect as written. Lemma 3 uses 1 - ||p|| - p_(C-1), whereas Appendix C derives 1 - ||p||² - p_(C-1); the printed bound can be negative. Also, the discussion after Lemma 2 incorrectly promotes maximal/minimal elements under Löwner order to greatest/least bounds. Other rank-one lower bounds need not be dominated by the leading-eigenvector bound.

The practical low-rank implementation lacks the guarantees claimed for its exact counterpart. Section 4.3 permits a fixed number of power iterations, but a Rayleigh quotient times an approximate eigenvector outer product need not remain a Löwner lower bound. No eigengap assumption, convergence tolerance, or approximation-error correction connects this implementation to Propositions 6 and 14.

The abstract's full-tensor quality claim exceeds the established result. Proposition 12 bounds relative variance only for diagonal entries. For Gaussian probes, an off-diagonal entry has variance F_ii F_jj + F_ij², so its relative standard deviation can diverge when F_ij approaches zero. Unbiasedness and a diagonal variance bound do not establish accurate full-matrix or inverse-Fisher estimation.

Several broader conclusions need qualification. Vanishing core approximation error as probabilities approach one-hot requires control of the changing Jacobian to imply vanishing network-space error. Comparing different error upper bounds also does not establish that one approximation has smaller actual error. These limitations matter because the theoretical guarantees constitute the paper's main contribution.

strengths: The estimator is simple and implementable: detached probability weights and random output probes yield an unbiased Fisher estimate through one backward pass, without explicitly constructing the parameter-output Jacobian.

Proposition 12 provides a useful, explicit diagonal variance characterization. Conditional on a fixed dataset, the coefficient of variation is bounded by sqrt(2), with a variance reduction for Rademacher probes relative to Gaussian probes.

The core-space analysis provides interpretable spectral bounds and transfers them to parameter space. Detailed appendices support most derivations, and the DistilBERT examples illustrate behavior in both untrained and fine-tuned classifiers.
weaknesses: Novelty is insufficiently established. The construction is a randomized outer-product estimate of a factored positive-semidefinite matrix, while many deterministic results follow directly from standard interlacing, trace, and congruence inequalities. The paper needs a precise comparison with existing stochastic curvature propagation and Fisher/generalized-Gauss–Newton estimators, including capabilities associated with the cited BackPACK and practical Gauss–Newton literature.

The Monte Carlo comparison in Section 4.1 mixes different sources of randomness. Its heavy-tailed counterexample concerns sampling inputs, whereas Proposition 12 conditions on the entire fixed dataset and averages only over probes. If the proposed estimator also uses sampled minibatches, input-sampling variance remains. At theta = 0 in the given binary example, the squared score is actually deterministic conditional on x. Thus this example does not establish the claimed advantage under matched sampling and computational assumptions.

The experiments are illustrative rather than validating. Figures 1 and 2 show marginal distributions of estimates on DistilBERT, but provide no exact-Fisher reference, quantitative estimation errors, repeated-run uncertainty, equal-budget Monte Carlo comparison, or runtime and memory measurements. With only four and two classes, exact reference calculations on selected parameters or smaller models would be feasible. Neither empirical bound tightness nor practical efficiency is convincingly demonstrated.

The scope of the quality guarantee is overstated. The bounded relative standard deviation is established for diagonal entries, not arbitrary full-matrix entries. For Gaussian probes, an off-diagonal estimate has variance F_ii F_jj + F_ij^2, so its relative standard deviation can diverge as F_ij approaches zero. Unbiasedness and rank-one storage also do not establish useful spectral accuracy or suitability for inversion; those claims require additional analysis.

Several mathematical statements need correction. Lemma 3 prints 1 - ||p|| - p_(C-1), whereas its proof requires 1 - ||p||^2 - p_(C-1); the printed bound can be negative even for a valid binary distribution. The discussion after Lemma 2 also conflates maximal/minimal elements with greatest/least bounds in the Löwner order. These are distinct claims, and the proof establishes only the weaker statements.

The practical significance remains uncertain. No downstream application establishes that these estimates improve optimization or another Fisher-based task, and the proposed accumulation along a changing training trajectory has no accompanying bias or tracking analysis. A theory-focused submission could compensate with stronger novelty and sharper guarantees, but the present theoretical and empirical evidence together fall below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computational problem: estimating neural-network Fisher information without explicitly constructing parameter-output Jacobians or the full matrix.

The main estimator in Eqs. (5)–(6) has a clear implementation using a detached probability weighting and one backward pass. Its unbiasedness and the diagonal variance formulas in Proposition 11 are well supported.
The core-space decomposition provides a useful framework for deriving deterministic bounds, and the appendices supply detailed proofs.

Experiments cover six model-task combinations spanning language, vision, and audio, with exact diagonal Fisher references. Table 2 reports substantially smaller errors than the empirical-Fisher baseline in several settings at comparable computational speed.
weaknesses: The exclusion of Monte Carlo baselines undermines the central efficiency comparison. Independently sampling one model label per input and differentiating the sum of their log probabilities yields a batch gradient whose outer product is unbiased for the batch Fisher: cross-example terms vanish because model scores have zero expectation. This also requires one backward pass. Its variance should be compared under matched computational budgets. Moreover, Section 4.1 attributes unbounded variance to input subsampling, whereas the proposed guarantee conditions on a fixed dataset; the latter does not eliminate input-sampling uncertainty.

The claimed novelty is insufficiently established. The main construction is random projection through a Fisher/Gauss–Newton factor, and its variance follows standard Gaussian/Rademacher fourth-moment identities. The paper needs a direct mathematical comparison with existing stochastic curvature propagation and Fisher/Gauss–Newton factor estimators. Much of the deterministic analysis follows standard interlacing, spectral truncation, and congruence inequalities, without quantitative comparisons supporting the claimed improvement over prior bounds.

The envelope interpretation following Lemma 2 is incorrect. The lemma establishes maximality/minimality under Löwner order, not a greatest rank-one lower bound or least diagonal upper bound. Distinct eigenvector-based rank-one lower bounds can be incomparable. Consequently, the repeated characterization of these bounds as globally tightest envelopes overstates the result.

There are explicit mathematical errors requiring correction. Lemma 3 states a bound involving 1−||p||−p_(C−1), whereas its proof requires 1−||p||²−p_(C−1); the stated expression is negative for p=(1/2,1/2). Equation (8) reuses the same probe ξ_x across eigencomponents, producing unwanted cross terms for k>1. Independent probes indexed by both input and eigencomponent are required. This also leaves the implementation underlying the rank-two results unclear.

The experimental interpretation overlooks exact rank constraints. For SST-2, the categorical core has rank one; for MNLI, it has rank two. Thus the corresponding full-rank core truncations are exact, rather than merely approximately low-rank because of fine-tuning. Their differences from the main estimator concern stochastic variance, numerical approximation, or implementation, and should be analyzed accordingly.

Evaluation and reproducibility remain incomplete. Results lack repeated-probe uncertainty, error-versus-compute curves, absolute runtimes, and sufficient implementation details. In particular, computing the defined empirical Fisher requires summing per-example gradient outer products; squaring a batch gradient generally computes a different quantity. The reported single-backward empirical-Fisher baseline needs clarification. The deterministic bounds also lack direct empirical tightness evaluation.

The broad claims about estimating the metric tensor exceed the demonstrated guarantees. The analysis and experiments primarily establish diagonal accuracy; a single full-matrix sample is rank one, and bounded diagonal relative variance does not establish useful spectral or inverse-Fisher accuracy. No downstream experiment demonstrates that the reported estimation gains improve optimization, pruning, or another intended application.

strengths: The main estimator in Eqs. (5)–(6) is unbiased, positive semidefinite, and implementable through one backward pass. Proposition 11 provides explicit diagonal variance formulas and a useful relative standard-deviation bound.
The core-space formulation organizes several useful spectral inequalities and their propagation through network Jacobians. Detailed proofs are supplied for the main results.

Experiments cover six model–task combinations across text, vision, and audio, comparing estimated diagonals against exact reference values. Table 2 shows promising accuracy at approximately the reported empirical-Fisher runtime.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison excludes an important inexpensive unbiased baseline on an incorrect computational premise. With independently sampled model labels for each example, the outer product of the summed batch score is unbiased for the batch Fisher: cross-example terms vanish because scores have zero expectation. This requires one backward pass. Its variance differs from the per-example Monte Carlo estimator, but it directly challenges the stated justification for excluding Monte Carlo methods. Furthermore, the empirical Fisher defined in the introduction is a sum of per-example outer products; squaring an ordinary batch gradient does not compute it. The one-pass empirical-Fisher implementation needs clarification.

Lemma 2 proves maximality/minimality among comparable matrices, not the claimed greatest rank-one lower bound or least diagonal upper bound. Distinct nonzero eigencomponents are incomparable rank-one lower bounds. For p=(0.8,0.2), both diag(p) and 0.32I upper-bound the core Fisher, but diag(p) is not below 0.32I. Thus the repeated characterization as 'envelopes' or 'tightest bounds,' used to motivate novelty, is incorrect.

The general low-rank estimator in Eq. (8) uses the same random variable ξ_x for all retained eigenvectors. For k>1 this leaves cross-eigenvector terms in its expectation, so it does not estimate the stated truncated Fisher. Independent probes indexed by both example and eigenvector are required. The prose suggests that this may be a notation error, but the appendix proves only k=1, leaving the LR(2) experiments insufficiently specified.

The claimed variance advantage mixes different sources of randomness. Section 4.1 considers sampling inputs from a heavy-tailed population, whereas Proposition 11 conditions on a fixed dataset and randomizes probes. Input-sampling variability would also affect the proposed method when estimating a population Fisher. The heavy-tail example therefore does not establish superiority under matched sampling and computational budgets.

Novelty is insufficiently established relative to stochastic Fisher/Gauss–Newton square-root estimation and curvature-propagation methods. The main construction is a random projection of weighted score vectors, and its variance calculation follows standard fourth-moment identities. Although related approximation libraries and methods are cited, the paper does not precisely distinguish its estimator from their stochastic curvature estimators or substantiate its claimed improvements over previous bounds.

Evaluation does not resolve the central practical questions: there are no repeated-run uncertainties, matched-budget comparisons against existing unbiased curvature estimators, or systematic probe-count and batch-size studies. Four configurations use randomly initialized classification heads. The explanation that low-rank accuracy on SST-2 and MNLI reflects fine-tuning is also confounded by their class counts: binary categorical Fisher matrices already have rank one, and three-class matrices have rank at most two. No downstream application validates the broader practical claims.

Several statements require correction or qualification. Lemma 3 omits the square on ||p|| in its first bound, unlike its proof, making the displayed claim false even for p=(0.5,0.5). The guaranteed relative variance concerns diagonal entries, not general off-diagonal relative error or full-matrix approximation quality. Overall, the useful main estimator does not outweigh the unresolved comparison, positioning, and correctness issues at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The main estimator is straightforward to implement through a scalar surrogate loss and one backward pass. Its unbiasedness and diagonal variance bound in Proposition 11 are clearly derived for a fixed dataset.
The core-space formulation provides a useful organization of Fisher approximations, with explicit spectral bounds and error bounds after propagation through the network Jacobian.

Experiments cover six model–dataset combinations across text, vision, and audio, using exact diagonal Fisher values as references. Table 2 reports promising accuracy at approximately the computational speed of the implemented empirical-Fisher baseline.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison has a major unresolved inconsistency. The empirical Fisher defined in the introduction sums per-example gradient outer products; an outer product of a single ordinary batch gradient includes cross-example terms and does not compute that quantity. Section 4.5 nevertheless treats empirical Fisher as requiring one backward pass while excluding Monte Carlo Fisher as requiring B passes. Moreover, independently sampling model labels and taking the outer product of the summed score gradient yields an unbiased batch-Fisher estimator in one backward pass because the scores have zero mean. This directly relevant baseline is missing.

The variance comparison changes the source of randomness. Section 4.1 demonstrates unbounded relative variance from sampling heavy-tailed inputs, whereas Proposition 11 conditions on a fixed dataset and averages only over probes. Sampling inputs or minibatches adds variance that the conditional bound does not control. Appendix A provides a relevant label-sampling argument, but it does not resolve the mismatched comparison in the main text.

Several mathematical claims need correction. Lemma 2 establishes maximality/minimality under the stated order constraints, not the claimed greatest rank-one lower bound or least diagonal upper bound; other feasible bounds can be incomparable. Lemma 3 prints 1−||p||−p_(C−1), whereas its proof requires the squared norm; the printed bound is negative for uniform binary probabilities. Equation (8) shares one probe across eigencomponents, introducing cross terms for k>1; independent probes indexed by both x and i are needed.

Novelty is insufficiently established relative to existing stochastic curvature propagation and Fisher/generalized-Gauss–Newton square-root methods. The estimator follows directly from randomized projection of a Fisher factor, and much of the deterministic analysis uses standard interlacing and matrix inequalities. The discussion of Botev et al. and BackPACK does not precisely distinguish the proposed contribution or provide corresponding comparisons.

The experiments lack repeated-probe uncertainty estimates, accuracy-versus-compute curves, and ablations over batch size and probe count. Four settings use randomly initialized classification heads, and no downstream application tests whether improved diagonal estimates provide practical benefits. On SST-2 the categorical core is exactly rank one, so the low-rank estimator's success there does not substantiate the claimed association between fine-tuning and approximate low rank.
